title: Woody Harrelson Turned Down Haymitch Offer Twice: I Didn’t ‘Think There Was Enough to Do’ in ‘The Hunger Games’
description: While a certain generation might associate Woody Harrelson most with his role as Haymitch Abernathy in the billion-dollar “Hunger Games” franchise,
body:
While a certain generation might associate Woody Harrelson most with his role as Haymitch Abernathy in the billion-dollar “Hunger Games” franchise, the actor has admitted he needed convincing to sign on for the dystopian film.

	During a recent Vanity Fair interview alongside his “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” co-star Joseph Zada (who plays a younger Abernathy in the prequel), Woody told the actor he “turned it down twice,” referring to the role.
	

	“Turned it down?” asked Zada. “Yeah, it’s stupid,” responded Harrelson. “I thought it was good, I read the books, really good, but I just don’t think there’s enough to do. I don’t know if there’s enough to do. It’s an arbitrary, odd way of assessing it.”

	He continued, explaining that director Gary Ross ultimately convinced him to do it. “[I] Can’t imagine not having had this experience in my life and knowing these people and then Gary calls me and he’s like, ‘Woody, you have to do this part. I don’t have a second choice. You have to play Haymitch.’ And he just talked to me for about 10 minutes on the phone. I’m like, ‘All right, okay, yeah, let’s do it.'”

	Released in 2012, Ross directed the first “Hunger Games” film, while Francis Lawrence went on to direct “Catching Fire,” “Mockingjay – Part 1,” “Mockingjay – Part 2,” “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and “Sunrise on the Reaping.” The recently released prequel takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more also star.
	

	In addition to Harrelson, who returned for the film, original cast members Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson also made small appearances. On an episode of “Call Her Daddy,” Lawrence told host Alex Cooper it was “unbelievable” to return as Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional.”

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” opened to $120 million at the box office last weekend, and is currently in theaters.

schema.headline: Woody Harrelson Turned Down Haymitch Offer Twice: I Didn’t ‘Think There Was Enough to Do’ in ‘The Hunger Games’

title: Interactive Films ‘The Run,’ ‘Kaiju Princess,’ ‘Back From the Other World’ Hit Taiwan Cinemas as Audiences Vote on Endings by Smartphone (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Moviegoers in Taiwan will be able to steer the outcome of three feature films with their phones, as interactive cinema outfit Next Interactive Stud
body:
Moviegoers in Taiwan will be able to steer the outcome of three feature films with their phones, as interactive cinema outfit Next Interactive Studio and exhibitor Showtime Cinemas roll out a run of titles opening one after another, starting Nov. 27 with English-language survival thriller “The Run.”

	Audiences scan a QR code on the screen to link their phones to a voting server in the auditorium. The majority pick at each decision point sets where the story goes next, including which characters survive and how the film ends. Once the lights come up, viewers can see a breakdown of the path they took, get a personality read and find other audience members who made the same calls.
	

	“The Run” is set on a remote trail in the mountains of northern Italy, where a fitness influencer with a worldwide following is pursued by masked killers. Audiences make snap decisions that decide whether she lives, and along the way bring a buried trauma to the surface. The film was cut down from 3.5 hours of footage into a theatrical version running 90 to 100 minutes, with five possible endings and 20 ways for her to die. It opens at Showtime’s flagship sites in Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung.

	Japanese live-action comedy “Back From the Other World” follows on Dec. 4. Adapted from a hit interactive game and produced with Fourth Wall, a creative team spanning Japan and Taiwan, the film is shot in the first person and casts the viewer as a hero who has slain demons in a fantasy realm, only to return to office life with his magic still working. Back at work, he discovers the goddesses he knew in that other world are now his bosses and co-workers. The cast includes Kawakita Saika and Uehara Ai.
	

	“Kaiju Princess,” set for the first quarter of 2027, is a first-person romance-adventure based on a popular Taiwanese game series and made in the style of tokusatsu, the Japanese special-effects genre. Starring Momonogi Kana and Unpai, the film – subtitled “Secret Pulse” – drops audiences into a world battered by giant-monster disasters. Group votes decide how humanity fights back against alien invaders and which romantic storylines play out. Its producers are again drawn from both Japan and Taiwan.

	Next Interactive is headed by founder Ronan Wong, who the company says has advised on, produced or distributed every interactive film to receive a commercial theatrical release, across both Western and Eastern markets. Wong served as interactive adviser on Japanese animated feature “Hypnosis Mic – Division Rap Battle,” which grossed JPY2.7 billion ($17 million) from fewer than 100 screens.

	“Interactive cinema transforms passive auditoriums into legendary, shared social arenas that simply cannot be replicated at home,” Wong said.

	He described the Taiwan launch as a major milestone for the company’s network. “As we prepare to bring these titles and our platform to global territories in 2027, we are proving that when audiences co-create the story together, cinema becomes an unmissable collective event,” Wong said.

	The company pitches itself to filmmakers, IP owners and exhibitors as a single partner covering both the production technology and the distribution needed to get interactive titles onto cinema screens. The Taiwan dates form part of a wider push across Asia, with releases in further international markets planned for 2027.

title: Shanghai Golden Goblet Winner Ridham Janve Stages a Goan Village Death Watch in ‘Goodbye Mr D’Mello’ at WAVES Film Bazaar
description: Ridham Janve, whose “Hunter’s Moon” won the Golden Goblet Award for best screenplay at the Shanghai International Film Festival this year, is bring
body:
Ridham Janve, whose “Hunter’s Moon” won the Golden Goblet Award for best screenplay at the Shanghai International Film Festival this year, is bringing “Goodbye Mr D’Mello,” a dark comedy set in a Goan village, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

	The film centers on an elderly professor who announces on his village WhatsApp group that he knows exactly when he is going to die, setting off a series of absurd reactions within the community. Through a colorful ensemble of characters, the film explores human curiosity, superstition, gossip, greed, faith and our uneasy relationship with mortality.
	

	“Living in Goa, I have been fascinated by the peculiarities of its social life, its people, humor and contradictions,” says Janve, who developed the screenplay with Goan journalist and writer Mayabhushan Nagvenkar. “There is also something fascinating about how traditional village gossip has found new life through WhatsApp and social media. It is also both amusing and disturbing about how easily another person’s private life can become a public spectacle.”

	Janve’s debut feature, “The Gold-Laden Sheep and the Sacred Mountain,” premiered at the International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR). His second, “Hunter’s Moon,” premiered in Shanghai.

	The film is being produced by Sharib Khan and Vikas Kumar through Khan & Kumar Media, alongside Nagvenkar through Mountain Motion Pictures, Janve’s production company. This is the producers’ second collaboration with Janve, following “Hunter’s Moon.”

	Kumar says, “We admire the passion and honesty of Ridham’s filmmaking. His first two features grew from years of close engagement with the Gaddi community in the Himalayas, and we have witnessed first-hand the care he takes to create worlds that feel genuinely lived-in. ‘Goodbye Mr D’Mello’ is very different in tone, but equally personal.”
	

	Khan & Kumar Media’s recent productions include “Sonsi” (“Shadow Bird”); “Songs of Forgotten Trees” (winner of the Horizons best director award, Venice Film Festival 2025); “Lovers in the Blue Night” (Venice Film Festival, Horizons section, Netpac award winner, 2026); and “The Ink-Stained Hand and the Missing Thumb” (Karlovy Vary International Film Festival, 2026).

	The producers plan to fund the film through co-producers, private financiers and institutional support. “Our production approach is lean and financially disciplined, drawing on existing locations, local resources and talent in Goa while maintaining the film’s creative ambitions,” says Kumar.

	Pre-production and shooting are planned for the first quarter of 2027. At Film Bazaar, the producers are looking to close the remaining financing and bring together creative and technical partners. “Beyond financing, we hope to build relationships with international collaborators, sales agents and distributors who can help the film reach audiences beyond India,” says Kumar.

	WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

title: LA Skins Fest Concludes 20th Year Celebrating Indigenous Artists
description: The 20th annual LA Skins Fest concluded on Sunday following the five-day celebration of Native American cinema and special screenings at the TCL Ch
body:
The 20th annual LA Skins Fest concluded on Sunday following the five-day celebration of Native American cinema and special screenings at the TCL Chinese Theatre.

	Since its founding, the festival has become a platform for Indigenous filmmakers to showcase their work, connect with entertainment industry professionals and reach new audiences. It also extends its mission outside the annual festival through its partnership with the Native American Media Alliance, supporting year-round professional development initiatives that includes writing labs, animation programs, showrunner training, development workshops and youth media education.
	

	This year’s LA Skins Fest featured a line-up of narrative features, documentaries, short films and special screenings that recognize Indigenous artists. This year’s festival opened with films presented by Amazon MGM Studios and also included a Netflix screening of “North of North” with actress Anna Lambe and a Cherokee-language screening of “The Rings of Power” followed by a discussion with the actors and Cherokee Film’s language revitalization team.

	The festival also began with a Native Youth Studio Tour at Sony Pictures Studios, providing students from Sherman Indian High School an introduction to career opportunities in media, which further reflects the festival’s dedication to supporting future generations of Native American entertainment professionals.

	Presented by Paramount Television Studios, the 15th Annual Native American Media Awards hosted by Q’orianka Kilcher and Kiowa Gordon concluded the festival with a celebration of Indigenous filmmakers, writers, actors and creative professionals. Among this year’s winners were Orlando Skidmore for achievement in filmmaking and Sophia Lindholm for achievement in student filmmaking. The emerging filmmaker award was given to Gina East for the narrative film category and Elissa Simons for the documentary category.
	

	The ceremony also recognized the 6th Annual Native American Writer Accelerator Grantees. Sponsored by Netflix, the program selects 12 Indigenous writers to receive financial assistance and opportunities to advance their careers in media. This year’s grantees are Doane Avery, Rachel Baldwin, Ripley Barnes, Sonny Brava, C.J. Caughman, Bryson Chun, Kelly Lynne D’Angelo, Yelyna DeLeon, Marleah Makpiaq LaBelle, Desiree Leiahloha, Jason Marcus and Vlad Perez.

title: Marathi Crime Drama ‘Hurda – That Tight Green Top’ Puts a Journalist’s Masculinity Under the Microscope at WAVES Film Bazaar
description: Apurv Gaikwad is presnting his debut feature “Hurda – That Tight Green Top,” a Marathi-language crime drama adapted from Atharva Pandit’s novel, to
body:
Apurv Gaikwad is presnting his debut feature “Hurda – That Tight Green Top,” a Marathi-language crime drama adapted from Atharva Pandit’s novel, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

	The film follows Chitranshu, a journalist investigating the mysterious deaths of three young sisters in a village in Maharashtra. When he returns to the village six years later, his search for the truth takes an unexpected turn, forcing him to confront uncomfortable realities.
	

	Gaikwad says he was drawn to the story because he “was fascinated by its polyphonic narrative, the way multiple characters coexist, each with their own distinct voice.” He adds, “Even months after reading the novel, there was one particular aspect of it that refused to leave me – the protagonist, Chitranshu.”

	“It is as much a mystery as it is a character study and an exploration of the society we live in. While the audience may find the answers they initially seek, I hope they leave the film with an entirely different set of questions,” says Gaikwad, who previously made the short mockumentary “The Last Auteur.”

	Gaikwad hopes to challenge the binary understanding of masculinity and “the comfortable distinction we make between good men and bad men. I hope the film encourages audiences to question their own prejudices and examine how caste, gender and social hierarchies shape their understanding of truth, justice and morality,” he says.

	The film is being produced by brothers Apurv and Akshay Gaikwad and Nina Bhatt of Disha Cinema and Khan & Kumar Media (“Songs of Forgotten Trees”). In an advanced stage of pre-production, the film is scheduled to start shooting in January 2027. Akassh Ghosalkar leads the cast, which also includes Rohit Kokate, Jitendra Lad, Gayatri Bansode and Gauri Deshpande. 
	

	Producer Nina Bhatt says she was drawn to Gaikwad’s examination of ordinary masculinity. “The contradictions between how men see themselves and how they exercise power in everyday relationships, his exploration of the entitlement and complicity that can exist within familiarity, affection and even empathy, felt particularly compelling to me. What made me want to back the project was his willingness to turn that examination inwards, rather than simply locate violence in others.”

	Producer Vikas Kumar says Khan & Kumar believes in nurturing and supporting new and important voices in cinema, and that he strongly believes Gaikwad is one of them. “Supporting ‘Hurda’ felt like a natural progression of that belief.”

	At Film Bazaar, the team hopes to engage with programmers, sales agents and other industry professionals and explore potential pathways for the independent production.

	WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

title: Bela Bajaria Reflects on Her Netflix Experience and Says ‘Stay Tuned’ at International Emmy Awards
description: Former Netflix executive Bela Bajaria put the emphasis on her belief in the transformative power of storytelling while accepting the Founders Award
body:
Former Netflix executive Bela Bajaria put the emphasis on her belief in the transformative power of storytelling while accepting the Founders Award Monday night at the International Emmy Awards in New York.

	Bajaria was ousted from her role as chief content officer of Netflix in a very public fashion last month amid a larger shake-up of content leadership at the streaming giant. In her speech — her first major public appearance since her departure — Bajaria reflected on her career journey to the top echelon of Hollywood as a senior executive at CBS and Universal Television before joining Netflix in 2016.
	

	In a nod to this week’s Thanksgiving holiday, Bajaria opened by expressing her gratitude for the opportunities she’s been afforded since her family relocated to Southern California in the late 1970s, when she was in grade school.

	“Gratitude isn’t passive or soft. It’s earned. Gratitude is strength in knowing nothing is guaranteed, and nothing can be taken for granted. Gratitude is the appreciation for both struggle and success, and sharing the journey with others,” Bajaria told the crowd.

	During most of the past decade, Bajaria was focused on building out Netflix’s local-language TV content operation at a scale never before seen in the industry. The experience was profound as the regional teams set off on a search for new creative voices.

	“Whether I was in Mumbai or Madrid, Bangkok or Berlin or anywhere in between — there’s nothing like being on the ground finding that original voice — in their homes, or sharing a meal, and looking eye to eye with openness, curiosity and respect,” Bajaria said. “I’ve seen firsthand how the saying is true: to paraphrase, you can ‘travel the world and never be a stranger.’ ”
	

	Bajaria indicated pride in the legacy of her role having greatly expanded the global village of television during her tenure at Netflix.

	“I’m full of gratitude for how far that idea — that belief — has forever transformed storytelling allover the world and not just in entertainment but in sports, brands and fandoms of all kinds,” she said. “Gratitude to all of you — you tell your stories from your own country and in your own language.Someone far away, who you will never meet, will watch and remember your work in the mostunexpected ways. You will stay with them forever.”

	Bajaria’s kudos were presented by Keri Russell, star of Netflix’s “The Diplomat,” and were preceded by a video with compliments on her leadership and creative instincts from such notable stars and creatives as Kate Hudson, Hasan Minhaj, Peter Morgan, Lee Sung Jin, Shonda Rhimes, Tan France, Ricardo Darín, Alex Pina, David Beckham and Hwang Dong-hyuk.

	In closing, Bajaria more than hinted to the audience that another chapter of her career is soon to come.

	“I’ve never been more excited for the next season. You know I love to surprise an audience,” she said. “So stay tuned.”

	Also honored during the event was Gerhard Zeiler, the former head of Germany’s RTL and former head of international for Time Warner and its successor companies. He exited Warner Bros. Discovery as part of the sale to Skydance and is preparing to mount a political run to lead Austria’s ruling Social Democratic Party. Zeiler’s Directorate Award was presented by former WBD chief executive David Zaslav.

	The BBC had a big night in the competitive awards. 

	The award for TV movie/miniseries was claimed by the BBC for “Prisoner 951,” from Dancing Ledge Productions, which tells the true story of a British-Iranian woman imprisoned in Iran for six years. The award for actor went to Bobby Schofield for his work in the searing BBC 2 family drama “Unforgivable,” from LA Productions.

	The Beeb also got the nod for documentary for “Louis Theroux: The Settlers,” from Mindhouse Productions. And it swept the children’s programming cateogies. Kids animation honor went to the “The Scarecrows Wedding,” produced by Magic Light Pictures. Live-action kid series went to “Dexter Procter: The 10-Year-Old Doctor,” produced by Terrible Productions and Various Artists Ltd. And the kids factual and entertainment kudo went to “Horrible Science,” produced by Lion Television.
	

	France’s historical drama “Carême” (VVZ / Shine Fiction) for Apple TV prevailed in the drama category. Turkey’s “Leyla” (Ay Yapim) won for telenovela.

	Comedy series honors went to Season 2 of Argentina’s “División Palermo [Community Squad]” (K&S Films / Netflix). The trophy for best actress went to Belgium’s Mona Mina Leon for the series “Holy Sh!t” (Fobic Films / Streamz).

	Nonscripted entertainment went to Season 2 of Channel 4’s “Educating Yorkshire,” from TwoFour.

	In the news heat, Sky News prevailed for its Ukraine documentary “The World: 24 Hours in the Kill Zone.”

	South Africa claimed sports documentary honors for “The Philipstown Wirecare Grand Prix,” produced by Giant Films.

	The current affairs category was taken by ITV’s  “Exposure: Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s War” (Zandland / ITV1).

	Belgium’s “De Klas van 2000 [The Class of 2000]” (De Mensen / DPG Media) won for short-form series.

	The arts programming award went to Germany’s “Der talentierte Mr. F” (Neue Flimmer GmbH on behalf of MDR / BR / ARD Kultur / RBB / HR)

title: Zosia Mamet Slams ‘Mad Men’ Boss Matthew Weiner as ‘Horrible’ Because He ‘Rules With Fear’: ‘He Dressed Me Down for 45 Minutes’
description: Zosia Mamet recently revealed that her “absolutely horrible” experience working with showrunner and producer Matthew Weiner on the set of “Mad Men”
body:
Zosia Mamet recently revealed that her “absolutely horrible” experience working with showrunner and producer Matthew Weiner on the set of “Mad Men” caused her to quit the series after just five episodes.

	“All the other actors were wonderful, but he really was like the Catholic Church back in the day, like that bro rules with fear,” she said while appearing on Dax Shepard’s “Armchair Expert” podcast on Monday. “He would dart every table read with this little speech… and he would talk about how he didn’t want any of us to take our scripts home… And he would be like, ‘If I see that, I’m going to find you, and I’m going to hunt you down. I’m going to kill you. Just kidding. Actually not. He would do this at every table read. And I was like, this not only isn’t funny, but it’s yucky. It’s fucking yucky, man.”
	

	Mamet, who appeared on Season 4 and 5 of the hit drama as Joyce Ramsay, then recounted the moment that pushed her to quit the show, explaining that “he came in and was having a bad day and decided to set his sights on me.” “During a block rehearsal, [he] just fucking went to town on me in front of the whole cast and crew… I called my agents when I left, and I was like, ‘I can’t go back to that set,’” she told Shepard. “He just systematically dressed me down for like 45 minutes. And I was like, ‘I want to kill myself.’”

	She continued: “My level of insecurity was so great that I knew that I wouldn’t be able [to]. I was like, I will shut down,” Mamet said. “I won’t be able to function in this environment, and the fear of that happening again was just too great.”
	

	The “Girls” actress had previously written about the showrunner in her 2025 essay collection, “Does This Make Me Funny?,” though she didn’t name him at the time. “I wrote an essay about it for my book where I don’t mention names,” Mamet said. “But I really wanted Matt Weiner to sue me because then he would be admitting to the fact that he knew I was writing about him.”

	Reps for Weiner did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

schema.headline: Zosia Mamet Slams ‘Mad Men’ Boss Matthew Weiner as ‘Horrible’ Because He ‘Rules With Fear’: ‘He Dressed Me Down for 45 Minutes’

title: ‘Michael’ Director Antoine Fuqua Accused of Assault, Battery by L.A. Bar Manager
description: “Michael” director Antoine Fuqua has been accused of assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress by a Los Angeles bar manager
body:
“Michael” director Antoine Fuqua has been accused of assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress by a Los Angeles bar manager following an incident back in February during which Fuqua allegedly pulled a gun on and struck the employee in the head.

	In a 10-page civil claim filed Friday in the Los Angeles Superior Court, William Rosenthal, an assistant manager at the bar Good Times at Davey Wayne’s, is said to have denied entry to Fuqua, his son, Brando, and his daughter because they were “visibly overly intoxicated.” Rosenthal was then spat on by a member of the group, to which Rosenthal told them they needed to leave the bar. 
	

	An hour later, Rosenthal alleges that Fuqua and his party remained standing outside the bar’s line, and upon noticing their presence, was approached by Fuqua and accused of pepper-spraying his daughter. When the manager denied the allegation, Fuqua “pulled out a handgun” and “struck” Rosenthal in the face before directing “a racial and antisemitic slur” at Rosenthal and threatening “to kill him.”

	“As Plaintiff staggered back in pain, Defendant Brando Fuqua appeared and approached Plaintiff and forcefully swung a handgun at Plaintiff’s face,” read the complaint. “Defendants Antoine Fuqua and Brandon Fuqua then pointed their handguns at Plaintiff, placing him in imminent fear for his life, before fleeing down the street.”

	Rosenthal is seeking $50,000 as a result of his suffering “serious physical and psychological injuries” which include a nose fracture, head injury, skin lacerations, post-traumatic stress disorder, severe emotional distress and severe scarring, all of which continue to cause him “great physical and mental pain and suffering.” The claim noted that Rosenthal believes said injuries “will result in some permanent disability.”
	

	Reps for Fuqua told Variety that “none of this is true.”

title: Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade at 100: Massive Minions, K-Pop Stars and ‘Sorcerer’s Apprentice’ Mickey Mouse
description: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is just two days away. Each year, thousands line the streets and millions more tune in around the country t
body:
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is just two days away. Each year, thousands line the streets and millions more tune in around the country to watch the iconic balloons, floats and performers parade through New York City. Titled “The Greatest Celebration,” this year’s event promises to go all out, featuring more balloons and brand-new floats among the festivities.

	It takes months of preparation and a village of creatives working behind the scenes to bring everything together. Variety has spent the last few months speaking with the team behind the magic and going inside the epic operation of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. 
	

	The floats are built in New Jersey at Macy’s Studios in Moonachie. The costumes and balloons are designed and also built. As the countdown begins, the balloons are tested, the rehearsals go into full effect and the finishing touches are added to the floats, while organizers appeal to the weather gods. But this is a well-oiled machine of artists who come prepared for the occasion. The parade debuted in 1924. This year, as it celebrates its 100th edition, Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production at Macy’s Studio, explains the heart of the parade begins with one thing: “storytelling.”


	
		May 2026	



	

					Tony Sarg’s marionette float
	



	When Variety caught up with Kennedy, he was already knee-deep in the design process and counting down to the big day. At this stage of planning, Kennedy and his team were collaborating with new partners and finalizing designs. The floats and balloons were in various stages of development — some still in the concept phase.

	“This time last year, I was starting on our first balloon for this year and we’ve been chipping away at that design-wise,” Kennedy explains. “This is just one part of the parade. There are so many aspects to it.” Kennedy noted that the team constantly pushes the boundaries of creativity, and this year is no exception. “Some classic characters are returning to the parade this year, which everyone will be super pumped for,” he says. Among them are Underdog, the Macy’s All-Stars Float and Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey.

	“It’s a massive deal for the folks at Disney,” Kennedy says. “It’s not an IP that generally comes out, except for a huge celebration. It’s our 100th parade, and they were really excited to join us. It was just a joy to get close to Mickey, but the Sorcerer’s Apprentice is so special. It’s that next level of elevated magic that blends really well with Macy’s.” 
	



	

	



	Kennedy also revealed that he and his team had been working on the Tony Sarg and the All-Stars float since the beginning of the year. Sarg, considered the godfather of American puppetry, designed the first six floats for the parade back in 1927. 

	This year, an entire Macy’s float will be dedicated to Sarg and his creations. 

	“There will be cold air inflatables, sculpts and puppets. It all takes place in this marionette theater where Tony Sarg himself is also represented as a marionette puppet,” Kennedy explains. “We’re still working on how the character comes across, but we are collaborating with Puppet Heap to bring those stories to life in a few interesting ways.” Kennedy acknowledges that not everyone may recognize Sarg’s name, which is why spotlighting him is so important. “This is the magician who brought us giant balloons,” he says.

	Another highlight is Snoopy, who returns to the parade in a new role as Joe Cool. “Joe Cool is what happens when Snoopy is pretending to be a student at school. He’s never been in the parade before in this form, which makes it really fun,” Kennedy said. “We’re excited to bring him and Woodstock together. I was on the Parade Studio floor yesterday and saw an arm and an ear being worked on.”



	

	



	
		July 2026	



	

					PJ Portera
	



	PJ Portera, the parade’s concept artist and specialist, is responsible for designing this year’s floats. 

	By July, Portera had already completed three and a half float designs, which were in various stages of production. “Those are all done on my end,” Portera says. “They’re on the floor now in different stages of production.” He also worked on one main balloon and a smaller one, both currently in production. “I’m doing pretty great for July 30,” he adds. Once a partner signs on, Portera and his team meet with them to brainstorm ideas. “They give us an idea of what they’re looking for — whether it’s for a balloon or a float — and we start with rough sketches, throwing ideas at the wall to see what sticks.” Afterward, the designs are reviewed by the engineering team to ensure feasibility before a final design is approved.

	Portera also oversaw the return of Doodlebug, a legacy float from the 1968 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. “We’ve been working on that for a while, even before the 2025 parade,” he says, tracing the design process back to February 2025. “It’s a 100-foot-long caterpillar-type float with room for someone to sit on top.” The idea came from John Cheney, a carpenter celebrating his 50th parade this year. “John has a huge history with the parade, and that’s where the Doodlebug idea was planted,” Portera explains. His approach was to look at previous versions and decide how closely to stay true to the original design while incorporating modern updates. Portera worked closely with the engineering team to ensure the design was feasible.

	“I had to ask, ‘Is this something that works in 2026 and what would it look like logistically to bring it to life?’” he says. Weather was also a significant consideration. “We had to ensure the designs could withstand snow and rain. A lot of that falls to engineering.”
	



	

	



	
		September 2026	



	

	



	With just 70 days to go, costume designer Kimberly Montgomery was in the thick of preparations. 

	This year’s parade will feature over 5,000 costumes. “Our goal is getting everything into production in these final days and ensuring everything is delivered on time,” Montgomery says. “When the costumes come in, it’s the most exciting part. It feels like Christmas when everything starts rolling in.” 

	Montgomery emphasized the importance of designing costumes that accommodate Macy’s employees, their friends and family members, who will wear them during the parade. “We have to make sure the costumes are comfortable for everyone, no matter their shape, size, height or weight.”

	As with every department, weather is a major factor, especially when it comes to costumes. “We have to consider whether the costumes are washable and if they can withstand rain,” Montgomery says, recalling the time in 2024 when it poured.

	“Everything in the warehouse was dripping wet when it came back the Friday after Thanksgiving. We’re ready for that if it happens again.” 

	Montgomery shares the enthusiasm of designing the costumes for the Tony Sarg float. The clown costumes, inspired by his designs, are brightly colored and reminiscent of the 1920s. She also oversees the 100 balloon handlers’ costumes, which involve collaboration with licensing teams to ensure accurate designs.

	Montgomery’s parade day starts at 4:15 a.m. “It’s a well-oiled machine,” she says. “We hire 200 to 250 people just for parade day to help dress everyone. Each person gets a picture of what the costume should look like, and then it’s go time!”
	



	

	



	
		November 2026	



	

	



	With less than 20 days to go, Kennedy is in Herald Square, preparing to flight-test all the new balloons. “It’s the first time outdoors,” he reveals. The floats are still receiving their finishing touches ahead of the Nov. 17 press preview. 

	“There’s a lot of talent logistics going on,” Kennedy adds. Performers will include singer and songwriter EJAE, RIIZE and more. The team is working closely with NBC to ensure the televised show is a hit.

	Billie Brightpaw will be making her debut as a featured balloon. “Billie Brightpaw is an all-new IP,” Kennedy explains. “You can get her as a plush, on ornaments, on jackets — she’s everywhere. She’s also going to be a live experience in Macy’s Herald Square, where you’ll be able to interact with her as a puppet. We’re launching that on Black Friday.”


	Kennedy is still most excited about the Tony Sarg float. “It came out so beautifully. It’s one of the most stunning things we’ve ever done,” he says. “The float has these amazing giant inflatables and a patina paint finish that really celebrates the history. The puppets we’ve been working on truly make it come alive. Seeing them in action for the first time — it’s like your brain shuts down, and you’re just a kid watching ‘Sesame Street.’”

	With the massive success of “Minions and Monsters” at the box office earlier this year, Buckaroo Bob the Minion will make an appearance. It’s a playful nod to “Dr. Strangelove.” The float features Bob the Minion wearing a cowboy hat and riding the biggest banana the parade has ever seen. “It’s a feat of modern science and technology, but also very silly,” Kennedy smiles. “People are going to love it.”

	A new Purina Float will feature puppet dogs. Kennedy shares, “The puppetry on this float is so clever, requiring someone to operate the dog from underneath the porch. It’s a great example of how we’re continuing to bring unexpected elements to the parade.”

	The DoorDash float recognizes the new partnership between the store and the delivery service. The team created a float that tells the story of quick delivery. “It includes a mini Macy’s,” Kennedy says. There are also hidden stories, and in an elaborate design move, it features a moving ride. He says, “The ride, which looks like a delivery vehicle, latches onto a track and circles the float. Kids will be riding in it, and it was a huge accomplishment to include a ride on a float.”

	The Macy’s All-Stars Float will also feature a live performance by K-pop boy band RIIZE. “It should be a wild moment,” Kennedy teases. “This float really pays tribute to the amazing parades that came before us while celebrating the characters people know and love.”



	

	



	As for 2027, Kennedy is already thinking ahead. “People are knocking down the door to be part of this celebration,” he says. “The answer is always about marching forward and looking up.”

title: Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?
description: After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music’s biggest sup
body:
After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music’s biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift. Instead, it was just a bad day for journalism. As attention-seeking magazine articles go, it’s hard to remember one that landed with quite such an unanticipated — but very loud — thud as “The Mastermind,” which has even hardened anti-Swifties wondering whether May Jeong slipped it through without editorial oversight, sneaking an alleged year’s worth of work onto the internet in the dead of morning.

	The alternative scenario was unthinkable. You would have to imagine that the author had actually been encouraged by editors to puzzle readers with a reported op-ed in which the subject of the piece — apparently, some top-tier celebrity! — is never named, yet still is subject to accusations that she picks her own friends, harbors ambitions, owned three pairs of Ugg boots while posing as a teenage commoner, and, most slanderously, was actually popular in school.

	When was the last time a high-profile magazine piece got ratio-ed this badly? That would have been one year and one week ago, when an exclusive excerpt from Olivia Nuzzi’s memoir, “American Canto,” was released to an incredulous world. And if there’s something that feels a little bit familiar about Jeong’s oddball tactic of not naming names in her piece (or at least not the big ones), it’s because this “you know who it’s about, but we’re not gonna say anyway” technique was a weird conceit last grafted into big-time American journalism by Nuzzi. That author referred to RFK only as “the Politician,” her ex-boyfriend as “the man I did not marry,” and so on. Nuzzi walked so that Jeong could run. Although this new piece is not any kind of roman a clef, she still feels compelled to euphemize Swift as “The Star,” her former label as “The Machine,” Scooter Braun as “The Manager,” Charli xcx as “The Brat” and even a secondary source as “The Person Familiar.”

	You would think Vanity Fair’s editors would recall the horrible reviews Nuzzi got for employing this gambit in “American Canto,” especially since the excerpt that introduced that annoying running gag to the world was published in… Vanity Fair. (How quickly they forget, but monthly journalism is a grind.)


	The article aims to unload secrets, but the secret we really need revealed is: Why do that? An interview with Jeong is in order. Or perhaps she is saving the rationale for her journalism class at Princeton, which may be the only one destined to have “The Mastermind” as curriculum. On first blush, a journalism non-pro might imagine that it was done to skirt libel laws, although that explanation holds no water, since the writer does quote several of her lowest-level sources by name, like the kids from Swift’s school who are ready to call her out now for not having been friendless or unmoneyed. (The former classmates will pick up some notoriety now, but will they regret that they could have become even more legendary if they’d been ID-ed as “The Girl Who Noticed The Star’s Uggs”?) No, it seems more likely that Jeong did it because we are, all of us, just archetypes in a fable. Except for the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High, who is un-archetypical enough to require a first and last name.


	Or perhaps Jeong refrains from naming Swift because she is the female equivalent of two other characters who are often referred to as He Who Must Not Be Named: Voldemort and Trump. Certainly the article seems to see Swift as an exemplor of the banality of evil, or, more to the point, a modern-day, real-life Regina George from “Mean Girls.” (No, not making that up, the journalist really goes with that.) Nearly every sentence is intended as a slap. Most journos writing a piece remotely in this vein — a reported one, as opposed to a straight opinion column — would try to leaven it at least once or twice with a positive or just neutral observation, before dropping the next bomb. “The Mastermind,” to its honest credit, dispenses with any such “See, I went into this with an open mind” niceties.
	

	The Star is found by The Writer to be “making herself a metonym for all women, successfully equat(ing) criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.” Compared to Katy Perry (aka “The California Girl”), who is “an adult pretending to be a child,” Swift “might be a child pretending to be an adult.” She “has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood.” For Swift, “all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism.” And then from there, Jeong gets to some of Swift’s bad qualities. (Just kidding.)

	If this were framed in any way as a commentary, as opposed to Vanity Fair objectively speaking in the voice of God, it wouldn’t catch much notice. But instead, the magazine frames it as an ultimate profile, the result of a year of work and talking to “over 100 sources.” We have to take the editors’ word for that, because the reportage as printed only quotes six sources on the record: the mother of a man who directed Swift in her school plays, a guitar teacher, a school music teacher, two girls who sat near Swift in music class, and a poet who is called in to assess how lyrics work. Five others are quoted anonymously: someone who used to be close to Swift, called The Person Familiar; a music pro called The Exec; a mystery ex-collaborator whose profession must be kept secret; a musician who toured with Swift; and a critic who was ostracized after slamming her… none of whom, even under the cloak of keeping their identities secret, have serious tea to spill. Now, reporters do often get great background information from interviews they don’t quote, so the 100-plus figure doesn’t sound completely unrealistic after so many months of reporting. But if these dozen or so sources were the best that the story had to actually quote — including a poet and a critic — you do have to wonder who the other 85-plus were, to be less quotable. (An editor’s introduction to the piece says one of the people interviewed was a “lover” of Swift’s, but we’ll just have to guess if the writer got to Joe Alwyn.)
	

	All that said, there are a handful of interesting questions and critical observations scattered through Jeong’s piece. (See? This is the part where you throw in something nice, to show you were objective.) If you removed the promise of fact-finding and this existed as an essay on Salon — RIP — you could credit her with some food-for-thought lines and decently amusing zingers. (Sure, I chuckled when Jeong, alluding to Travis Kelce, wrote, “Regretfully we must call him Redwood.”)

	But the veneer of investigative reporting placed upon this piece mostly shows just how low the bar is for an attempted expose anymore. Even without the terminally twee names. It’d be nice to suppose that Jeong really did come up with something after a year — there is so much hinted at that is quickly dropped — and that Vanity Fair’s lawyers gutted a more substantial piece to within an inch of a life. But more probably, it’s an example of snark masquerading as reportage. And it shows again that some journalists (even journalists that teach at Princeton) are too quick, when an expensive. exhaustive fishing expedition fails to turn up much, to succumb to a sad maxim: If you can’t get the goods, just get cute. But don’t expect readers who expect more out of their hit squads not to notice.

schema.headline: Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?

              Devin Ratray might wanna save Macaulay Culkin a slice of cheese pizza this time around ... 'cause the "Home Alone" star is down to reprise his role as Buzz in the new sequel, despite being left in the dark about the project ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
              Devin, who famously played Kevin McCallister's obnoxious older brother in the OG Christmas classic, tells TMZ ... he hasn't been given any information about the new movie, but he's down to do whatever is asked of him to ensure the "Home Alone" legacy continues in a positive way.
      
    
              Turns out, Buzz isn't the only one who hasn't gotten the memo. As we previously reported ... Christopher Columbus, who directed the first two "Home Alone" movies, also wasn't clued in on the new sequel.
      
    
              Devin's no stranger to stepping back into Buzz's shoes ... he reprised his role in 2021's "Home Sweet Home Alone," where fans learned Kevin's childhood tormentor had grown up to become a cop.
      
    
              We'll see if Macaulay gives his big bro a ring ... but something tells us Kevin still hasn't forgiven him for eating all that cheese pizza!!!

title: Gavin Newsom Blasted By Mother of Murdered 8-Year-Old After Commuting Death Row Sentences
description:
Gavin Newsom
                          Berated by Mother of 8-Year-Old Murder Victim ...
body:
Gavin Newsom
                          Berated by Mother of 8-Year-Old Murder Victim ...
                          My Son Deserved A Better Governor!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 23, 2026
                            6:30 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Gavin Newsom was raked over the coals by the mother of a murdered 8-year-old and several other family members of victims after he commuted the sentences of all of California's death row inmates.
      
    
              Here's the deal ... earlier this month, Governor Newsom commuted all 548 death row inmates -- changing their punishment from death to life in prison.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              President Donald Trump, looking to shame the governor for his choice, hosted family members of several victims at an event Monday ... at which he called out Newsom for standing with "the murderers and the child slayers."
      

              The prez then handed off the mic to Sandy Friend ... whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was sexually assaulted, tortured and killed by Robert Boyd Rhoades in 1996.
      
    
              Rhoades was sentenced to death, but it was never carried out ... and the commutation means he will now serve a life sentence instead.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              At the podium, Sally spoke directly to Newsom ... saying, "Face me, Governor Newsom. Tell me Michael’s life doesn’t matter. Michael deserved a governor who would stand with the victims, honor their justice, and respect the will of the people.”
      
    
              Other victims -- including the family of a slain police detective and the father of 12-year-old Polly Klaas, who was strangled to death in 1996 -- also ripped into the governor.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              It's worth noting ... the last time a California inmate was executed was 2006 -- though California voters chose not to abolish it at least twice since then.
      
    
              In a statement to the New York Post, Governor Newsom said, "To the families standing with him today: your grief is real. Every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. Not one walks out. Donald Trump’s criminals walk out.”

              Dax and Kristen have been married since 2013 ... and share two daughters.

title: Actress Zosia Mamet Dives Into Famous Dad's Pro-Trump Views
description:
Actress Zosia Mamet
                          My Famous Pops Loves Trump
body:
Actress Zosia Mamet
                          My Famous Pops Loves Trump
                          ... But I Think He's Just Being A Contrarian
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 23, 2026
                            6:05 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              Zosia Mamet says her famous father's pro-Trump views drive her and her sister crazy ... admitting her sister called her in tears when she learned he'd be honored by the Kennedy Center.
      
    
              The "Girls" actress appeared on Dax Shepherd's "Armchair Expert" podcast ... and Dax brought up her dad David Mamet's conservative leanings.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              If you don't know, David -- a playwright best known for writing "Glengarry Glen Ross" -- is an ardent supporter of the president ... endorsing him in 2020 and 2024.
      

              Zosia says her dad isn't screwing with people like Dax thought at first ... though she admits she sometimes thinks he'll say things just to be contrarian -- even when they go against his own beliefs.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              She says he's being honored at the Kennedy Center ... which has a more political tilt to it than it used to, ever since President Donald Trump became the foundation's chairman. While a great honor for her father, Zosia says one of her sisters called her crying just the other day when she found out about it.
      
    
              Zosia says her sister told her, "It's not fair! Everybody else's 80-year-old dad loves Trump, but they're not famous."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Zosia says she ultimately still loves her dad ... adding he's a great hang -- and definitely one of the smartest people she knows.
      
    
              With Thanksgiving right around the corner, it's nice to know even celebs might have some awkward political chats around the table this holiday season!
